title: The Harvest of the Ninth Floor
premise: When Paloma Ishikawa takes a teaching job at Hollowmere Primary, they recognize the school's pattern of vanishing students—it mirrors the disappearances from their grandmother's apartment building in 1974, the year grandma's photographs first gained a ninth chair. The chair belongs to something that has been trading children for decades, feeding on the memories of those who forget them, and it has finally claimed Paloma's niece. To end the harvest, Paloma must descend into the building's impossible ninth floor, where the taken are preserved as living memories, and give back what their family stole in 1974: the name of the entity's first victim, erased so thoroughly that even it cannot remember who it lost. In the climax, Paloma sacrifices their own memories of grandma to restore the erased child, unmaking the bargain and collapsing the ninth floor. The children return, but Paloma is left with a photograph of a grandmother they no longer recognize—and a chair that is finally just a chair.
about_author: August Sterling is the pen name of a former night-shift school custodian who spent eleven years convinced the boiler room had a tenth floor. They write horror about institutions that remember too much and families that remember too little. Sterling lives in a coastal town where the fog arrives on schedule and is, they insist, only fog.

chapters.title: The Extra Chair
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. While sorting grandma's estate, Paloma notices every photograph since 1974 contains a ninth dining chair that no one else can see. When they touch the photo, the room tilts and they smell chalk dust and old carpet. The beat is quiet dread: the past has been waiting for them to look.

chapters.title: First Bell at Hollowmere
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. They begin teaching Year Six at Hollowmere Primary, where the staff are aggressively cheerful and classroom 4C has been 'under renovation' for nine years. A student, Wren, asks why the school photo has a blank space where a boy used to stand. Beat: unease dressed as normalcy.

chapters.title: Attendance
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. Cross-referencing old registers, Paloma finds Hollowmere has lost one student roughly every six years since 1974—always from Year Six, always mid-term, always erased from records within a month. The headmistress, Ms. Aldery, warns them off gently, then not so gently. Beat: the first hard evidence, and the first threat.

chapters.title: What Grandma Kept
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV, with grandma's 1974 diary in flashback. The diary describes the apartment building's 'ninth floor'—a floor that doesn't exist—and a neighbor's son who came back wrong, smiling, forgetting his own mother. The final entry is torn out. Beat: Paloma realizes this is inheritance, not coincidence.

chapters.title: The Boy in 4C
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren stays late and sees a boy in the sealed classroom, standing at a desk, mouthing numbers. When she blinks, he's closer. She tells Paloma, who recognizes the boy from grandma's photographs. Beat: the past and present touch, and a child is now in danger.

chapters.title: Six Years, Six Children
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. Paloma tracks the six taken children across decades: one drowned, one institutionalized, one never found. All their families lived in grandma's building. All their parents eventually stopped grieving—too completely. Beat: horror shifts from the entity to the forgetting itself.

chapters.title: Ms. Aldery's Office
chapters.summary: Aldery's POV. The headmistress reveals she was a classmate of the 1974 children and has spent her career feeding the school's 'arrangement'—cooperation in exchange for the building's strange stability. She offers Paloma a choice: forget, like everyone else. Beat: power's corruption made intimate and reasonable.

chapters.title: The Torn Page
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. Paloma finds the torn diary page hidden in grandma's sewing box: a list of nine names, the ninth burned away, with the words 'we agreed to give it one and it agreed to stop at one.' The 1974 tenants made a bargain—and someone broke it. Beat: the family's guilt surfaces.

chapters.title: Wren's Drawing
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren draws the boy from 4C and adds a ninth figure she insists was 'already in the picture': a small child holding a chair. That night her bedroom window is found open from the inside. Beat: the harvest has chosen its next, and Paloma's protective fury ignites.

chapters.title: Missing
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. Wren is gone, and by morning so is every trace she ever attended Hollowmere—except in Paloma's memory, which the thing cannot yet reach. Aldery, shaken, admits the bargain is failing and the entity is taking more than agreed. Beat: isolation, urgency, and a reluctant ally.

chapters.title: The Ninth Floor
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. Following the diary's instructions, Paloma rides grandma's building's elevator past eight and steps out into a corridor of classroom doors stretching into dark, each labeled with a taken child's name. Behind every door, a life continues, frozen mid-morning. Beat: awe and terror—the taken are not dead, but stored.

chapters.title: The Boy Who Waited
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. Paloma finds the boy from 4C, Tomas, who has been nine years old for fifty years and remembers everything, including the name of the erased ninth child—almost. He can only say it 'tastes like' Paloma's family. Beat: hope with a hook; the answer is in Paloma's own blood.

chapters.title: The Keeper
chapters.summary: The Keeper's POV, fragmented and hungry. The entity that tends the ninth floor was once a child itself, taken in a bargain older than the building, sustained by memories fed to it. It senses Paloma's intact memory as an insult and a meal. Beat: the antagonist's tragic, corrupting logic.

chapters.title: What the Family Took
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. In grandma's locked flat, Paloma finds a hidden room behind the wardrobe: the ninth chair, real, and beneath its cushion a birth certificate for a child no record elsewhere acknowledges—Paloma's aunt, erased in 1974 when the family chose to save their own son. Beat: the gut-punch; the debt is personal.

chapters.title: Aunt Nobody
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV, interwoven with grandma's final lucid days in flashback. Dying, grandma almost said the name, and the room grew cold, and she chose silence again. Paloma understands: every forgetting was a fresh payment, and grandma paid with her granddaughter's future. Beat: grief weaponized into resolve.

chapters.title: Aldery's Confession
chapters.summary: Aldery's POV. Aldery reveals she was the one who proposed the 1974 bargain and has renewed it six times, each renewal costing her a memory she can't name. She gives Paloma the school's oldest register—the entity's own ledger—before the building begins to notice her treason. Beat: complicity, then sacrifice.

chapters.title: The Ledger
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. The register lists every harvest in the Keeper's hand, and on the first page, a name burned away but pressed deep enough into the paper to read by touch: 'Mari Ishikawa.' The Keeper's first victim was Paloma's own aunt—taken, not erased, and then erased from memory to hide the crime. Beat: everything converges.

chapters.title: Doors Opening
chapters.summary: Tomas's POV. The ninth floor begins to decay as the Keeper hunts Paloma; classroom doors swing open and the frozen children wake, fifty years hungry for morning. Tomas leads them toward the elevator, choosing to be brave for the first time since 1974. Beat: the stored lives rise, and hope becomes momentum.

chapters.title: The Chair at the Table
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. Paloma carries the ninth chair into the ninth floor's central classroom and sets it at the table where the Keeper waits, wearing the accumulated faces of everyone it has fed on. It offers Wren's life for Paloma's memories. Beat: the temptation of the cheap bargain, refused.

chapters.title: Say Her Name
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. Paloma begins speaking their memories of grandma aloud—every one—as payment and proof, and with each memory surrendered, the burned name on the ledger darkens. The Keeper falters, because remembering Mari means admitting what was done to it. Beat: the climax's terrible exchange, memory by memory.

chapters.title: Mari Ishikawa
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. The name completes, and Mari steps out of the ledger as a nine-year-old girl with her family's face, and the Keeper—unmasked as the first bargain's other forgotten child—collapses into the chair and is finally, simply, a chair. The floor folds shut around them. Beat: release, and the cost: Paloma can no longer picture grandma at all.

chapters.title: Morning Roll Call
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. Weeks later: Wren is back, Tomas is a fifty-year-old man learning to grieve his lost life, and classroom 4C is finally just a room. Paloma keeps grandma's photograph on their desk, the ninth chair gone, and though they can't remember her face, they keep her teacup filled anyway. Beat: belonging rebuilt on honest loss—some things you return; some you carry without understanding.
